---
order: 9
unit: challenge
title: "Challenge: prepare a talk"
shape: speech
summary: "Students prepare a one-minute talk for a real audience in five parts: plan it, write the script, cut it to cue cards, rehearse with a partner and give it in class, then check the talk against the plan. The site plans, scripts and checks. Rehearsing and presenting happen in class, and a partner or the teacher judges the delivery."
language: maths
node: [AC9E4LY07 n3, AC9E6LY07 n3, AC9E8LY07 n1, AC9E8LY07 n2]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A plan for a one-minute talk: an opening, two points with a detail each, and a close." }
hook: "A talk is a few minutes of speaking and a lot of choices behind it. Can you make every one of them on purpose?"
---
You will prepare a talk of about one minute for your class. Choose one change you would like to see in your school, such as the length of lunch, a new place to sit, or a club. Your listeners are your class, and your aim is for them to agree to try it.

You will use what you have learned in this course: a plan with a point, a script written for the ear, cue cards, a register that suits the listeners, a voice and visuals on purpose, and feedback from a rehearsal. The site helps you plan, script and check. **You give the talk in class**, to your teacher and your classmates. Nobody here can hear it, so a partner or your teacher judges the delivery.

## Purpose and audience: what will go wrong?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Predicting what a listener says after a talk that ignores most of the course draws the earlier lessons together before students prepare their own."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Nib reads a full script word for word from the page, in the same flat voice from start to finish, with slides that repeat every sentence. What will a classmate most likely say afterwards?"
  options: ["It was clear because everything was said twice", "It felt like being read to, and I stopped listening part way through", "It was too short", "It was too exciting to follow"]
  actual: "It felt like being read to, and I stopped listening part way through. A talk read from the page with one voice and slides that repeat it gives listeners little to listen for. Each part of this challenge fixes one of those problems."
```

## Plan: opening, points, details and close

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Writing a plan for a talk on a chosen change in the school puts the aim, the audience and the four parts of a plan together."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#plan", height: 520 }
hint: ["What do you want your class to do after your talk?", "Which fact or example makes each point believable?"]
check: { type: board, text: "Write a line for each part of your plan: an opening, three points that each have a detail, and a close. Label each one. Every line needs words in it.", when: "n_empty = 0 and n_right = 8", explain: "Every line has words and a label. Say your aim in one sentence to a partner: 'After my talk, my class will …'." }
```

The board checks that every line has words and a label. Whether the plan suits your class is for a partner or your teacher to judge.

## Script: write it to be heard

In your own document, write the opening and your first point as a script. Use four or more sentences, none of them 15 words or longer. Use at least one joining word such as *because*, *when* or *until*. Choose words and a register that suit your class.

Here is one example, from Nib's lunch talk: "Who here has ever wished lunch were a bit longer? Today I want to show you how to get ten more minutes. **First**, the queue wastes time. Last week the last student was served after nine minutes. That is nine minutes of lunch gone, **because** the line is slow."

Then say your script aloud to a partner. Could you say each sentence in one breath? Did your partner follow it the first time? Does your register suit your class?

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing the opening and first point of the script in their own document, then saying it aloud, shows whether the script is built for the ear, which only a spoken test can tell."
hint: ["Could you say each sentence in one breath?", "Which signpost word will tell your listeners where they are?"]
check: { type: reflect, text: "I wrote the opening and my first point as four or more short sentences with at least one joining word, and a partner could follow it when I said it aloud." }
```

## Cue cards: say it, don't read it

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Cutting a script to cue cards with the limits from the cue-card lesson turns the written script into something a speaker can say."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#cards", height: 640 }
hint: ["Which words would bring each part back?", "Which number or name must be right?"]
check: { type: board, text: "Pick key words so that every section has a card, no card holds more than 8 words, and the key words are no more than a quarter of the script.", when: "n_cards = n_sections and n_over = 0 and key_pct <= 25", explain: "The board counts a card in every section, none over 8 words, and key words at or below a quarter of the script. Press Print cue cards, cut them out and keep them for the rehearsal." }
```

The board has a script to practise on. To use your own, press **Use my own script**, paste it with one paragraph for each part, then press **Done writing**. **Print cue cards** makes the cards.

## Features: choose a voice and a visual

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Choosing one voice setting and one visual for the talk, and justifying each for the listeners, is the plan-and-justify part of AC9E8LY07 n1 and is compared with models, not marked."
check:
  type: reasoning
  q: "Choose one voice setting (pace, volume, pitch or tone) and one visual for your talk. For each, say where in your talk you will use it, and why it suits your purpose and your listeners."
  placeholder: "I will slow down at ... because ... My visual is ... It adds ... for my listeners because ..."
  models:
    - title: "A strong answer"
      text: "Voice: I will slow down and get a little louder on 'one more window', because it is the request and I want my class to catch it. Visual: a bar chart of how long the queue takes each day, shown in point one. It adds the pattern, which my words would take too long to say, and it helps my class see that the problem is real."
    - title: "A different plan that also works"
      text: "Voice: I will use a warm, steady tone in my opening, because I want my class to feel I am on their side. Visual: a simple drawing of the canteen with the spare window marked, shown in point two. It adds the layout, so listeners can picture where the window is."
  criteria: ["I chose a voice setting and a visual.", "I said where in my talk each goes.", "I said why each suits my purpose and my listeners."]
  explain: "There is no one right plan. What matters is that each choice is made on purpose and has a reason that links it to the listeners."
```

## Rehearse: with a partner, in class

```step
stage: practise
insight: "The rehearsal happens in class. The step is the student's own report that they rehearsed with a partner, used the checklist and changed one thing."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I rehearsed my talk with a partner in class, listened to their feedback on the checklist, changed one thing and said it again." }
```

Use the same checklist as in the rehearsal lesson. Your partner ticks what they heard and saw, and writes one thing to keep and one to change.

- I could hear every word, including the last sentence.
- The speaker looked up from the cards for most of the talk.
- The speaker slowed down or paused on the most important part.
- The speaker's tone matched the words.
- One thing to keep: …
- One thing to change: …

Your teacher can tell you what is allowed in your class.

## Present and check: against your plan

```step
stage: info
insight: "Comparing what the student planned with what happened, after the talk is given in class, builds the habit of reflecting on the effect of voice choices."
check:
  type: reasoning
  q: "After you have given your talk in class, check it against your plan. Choose one voice choice you meant to make. Say what you meant it to do for your listeners, what it did, and what you would change next time."
  placeholder: "I meant to ... I wanted my listeners to ... What happened was ... Next time I would ..."
  models:
    - title: "A strong answer"
      text: "I meant to slow down and pause before my close, 'Please try a quiet corner for a week.' I wanted my listeners to catch the request. What happened was that I paused, but I also sped up again straight after and some of the class looked away. Next time I would stay slow for the whole last sentence."
    - title: "A different choice that also works"
      text: "I meant to look up from my cards for the whole of point two. I wanted my listeners to feel I was talking to them. What happened was that I looked up for the first half and then read the cards again when I forgot a number. Next time I would put the number on the card in large print."
  criteria: ["I named one choice I meant to make.", "I said what it did for my listeners.", "I said what I would change next time."]
  explain: "There is no one right answer. What matters is that you compare what you meant with what happened, and decide what to change."
```

## Wider: another talk

```step
stage: info
tier: wider
insight: "Planning a talk for a different purpose keeps the skill and shows how the plan changes with the purpose."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I planned a second talk for a different purpose, such as to inform or to entertain, and said what I changed in the plan." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students plan, script and cut down a one-minute talk on a change they
  would like to see in the school, rehearse it with a partner in class, give it
  in class, and check what they did against what they planned. The site plans,
  scripts and checks; delivery is yours to see.
time: 60
timing: Predict and plan 12 min · Script 12 min · Cue cards 10 min · Rehearse in
  class 12 min · Present in class (over one or two lessons) · Check against the
  plan 8 min
goals:
  - I can plan, script and cut down a short talk for a real audience.
  - I can rehearse it with a partner and change one thing because of their
    feedback.
  - I can compare what I meant my voice to do with what it did.
struggle: Students prepare well and then read the script. Ask them to put the
  script away before they present; the cards are the only page in their hand.
before: >
  Do the plan board yourself with a topic of your own, then print the cards.


  The one idea: the whole course in one piece of work. This lesson is tagged
  AC9E4LY07 node 3, AC9E6LY07 node 3 and AC9E8LY07 node 2, which are about
  **delivering** a talk, and AC9E8LY07 node 1, whose plan-and-justify part is
  the Features step (the register lesson is the other half). **The site covers
  the preparing and the self-check; you see the delivery.** Nothing here listens
  to a talk, and no step records one. Tick the node's criteria from what you see
  and hear in class: a clear structure with an opening and a close, at least one
  complex sentence said aloud, at least one deliberate voice choice (pace,
  volume, pitch or tone varied for effect), a theme with at least three
  supporting points (the plan board asks for three), and a precise topic word or
  two (nothing on the site teaches or checks topic vocabulary beyond the key
  words on the cards; this part of AC9E6LY07 node 3 is yours to hear). The
  script is written in the student's own document and nothing checks it, so look
  for at least one complex sentence when you read it, and listen for whether it
  is said aloud. The student's reasoning at the end gives their own account of
  the intended and actual effect of one voice choice, which is what AC9E8LY07
  node 2 asks them to reflect on. A partial-coverage marker for steps like these
  is proposed in roadmap/english.md.


  Choose the audience (the class, a Year 5 buddy class, parents at an event) and
  the time (about a minute). Students choose a change for the school, so the
  topic is theirs; no one is asked anything personal. Keep topics low-stakes and
  school-based. Nib's lunch example in the plan and cards boards is made up for
  the lesson.


  What the boards count: the plan board counts filled lines and correct labels
  (a student could type anything, so read the plans); the cue board counts
  cards, words per card (limit 8) and key words as a share of the script (a
  quarter at most). Neither judges the content. The script step has no board:
  students write it in their own document and a partner or you read it. Whether
  the plan suits the class, whether the register fits and whether the script
  sounds natural are for a partner or you to judge by listening. Students paste
  their script into the cue board to cut it down.


  Print cue cards gives index cards two across a page. Print highlighted script
  is there for a student who needs more on the page.
running:
  - "Predict: ask which of the earlier lessons the listener's verdict is about."
  - "Plan: partners say the aim back. If they cannot, it needs fixing before the
    script."
  - "Script: students read it aloud once, quietly, and mark where they run out
    of breath."
  - "Cue cards: cover the script and say one part from the cards. Add a word
    where they got stuck."
  - "Rehearse: pairs use the checklist, then change one thing and say it again.
    In class."
  - "Present: each student gives the talk, from cards. Listeners use the
    checklist. Allow a second go for anyone who wants it."
  - "Check: the reasoning step is written after presenting. Read a few to see
    what students noticed about their own voice."
stuck:
  - see: A student reads the script aloud, word for word, when presenting.
    ask: What are the cards for?
    fix: Put the script away. Cards only. Pause and look up between parts.
  - see: A student's talk runs well over the time.
    ask: Which point would your listeners miss least?
    fix: Cut a point or a detail. A shorter talk said well is better.
  - see: A student freezes when presenting.
    ask: What is the first key word on your first card?
    fix: Offer a second go, perhaps to a partner first. Do not press.
stretch: Give the talk a second time to a different audience, such as Year 5,
  and change the register and one visual.
support: The cue board's sample script, a checklist card, and a partner who
  listens first. Rehearse to a partner before the class.
leads: >
  Next: the course Discussion moves (planned) takes the same attention to
  listeners into talk with others.


  The same preparing steps work for any subject's oral task: a science report, a
  history talk, a drama monologue.
exit:
  q: Name one choice you made in your talk and say what you meant it to do for
    your listeners.
  a: "Any choice with its reason: 'I slowed down at the close so the request would
    be heard.'"
explain: >
  A talk is prepared in steps: a **plan** with an aim, a **script** written for
  the ear, **cue cards** with the key words, a **rehearsal** with a partner and
  one change.


  Then you **present** and **check** what you meant against what happened.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: What makes a talk worth listening to?
    prompts:
      - Think of a talk at assembly that you remember. What did the speaker do?
      - What did they not do?
    notes: Students name a clear point, a voice that varied and a speaker who looked
      up. These are the things the course has covered.
  activities:
    - at: investigate
      kind: activity
      title: Say your aim
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Partners read each other's plan and say the aim back: 'After this talk,
        my class will …'. If they cannot, the plan needs an aim.
      notes: This catches talks that are only topics. Fix the aim before the script.
    - at: end
      kind: activity
      title: Rehearse and change one thing
      minutes: 12
      do: >
        Pairs rehearse from their cards. The listener uses the checklist and
        writes one thing to keep and one to change. The speaker changes one
        thing and says it again. Then the pair swap.
      notes: Stop any pair whose feedback is only 'good'. Ask 'what did you hear, and
        where?'.
    - at: end
      kind: activity
      title: Give the talk
      minutes: 20
      do: >
        Each student gives their talk from cards. Listeners use the checklist
        and give one specific comment to each speaker, in pairs afterwards or on
        a slip.
      notes: Keep it low-stakes and supportive. Offer a second go. Tick the delivery
        criteria from what you see and hear.
  questions:
    - at: end
      title: Which part failed?
      type: question
      q: A listener says, 'Your talk was well planned, but I couldn't tell what you
        wanted us to do.' Which part of the plan most needs fixing?
      options:
        - The opening, because it came first
        - The details, because there were too few
        - The close, because it should say what listeners should do
        - The register, because it was too formal
      answer: 2
      feedback:
        - The opening tells listeners what the talk is about. It does not
          usually say what to do.
        - Details back up points. The problem here is the request.
        - null
        - Register is about how formal the talk sounds. The listener's problem
          is the ask.
      explain: The close says the main idea again and tells listeners what to do. If
        listeners cannot say what was asked, the close needs fixing.
```

s opening: Ask the class who has ever wished lunch were a bit longer. Then say there is a simple way to get ten more minutes.
s point: First, the lunch queue wastes time.
s detail: Last week it took nine minutes for the last student to be served.
s point: Second, a second serving window would fix it.
s detail: The canteen has a spare window that is never opened.
s point: Third, helpers are easy to find.
s detail: Two Year 10 volunteers have offered to serve.
s close: Say it again: queue, window, helpers. Then ask the class to support the idea.
# endregion



# region: cards
widget: cohesion
mode: cue
max: 8
tools: write
p opening: Who here has ever wished lunch were a bit longer? Today I want to show you how to get ten more minutes.
p point1: First, the queue wastes time. Last week the last student was served after nine minutes. That is nine minutes of lunch gone.
p point2: Second, a second serving window would fix it. The canteen has a spare window that is never opened, and two helpers could run it.
p close: So please back the idea. One more window, ten more minutes, and a lunch that is really a lunch.
# endregion
